title: Built an algo trading fleet with 5 bots (rules-based + LLM-driven) — here's the honest post-mortem after 6 weeks of sandbox trading
author: hikewithcaramel
selftext:
Been running a multi-strategy trading system on IG Markets for about 6 weeks — sharing the real numbers, not a highlight reel.

The fleet:

V3 — regime-classifying bot (ADX/Hurst), switches between trend-following and mean-reversion

AGENT — pure deterministic rules engine, no AI in the trading decisions

SCALP+TREND — two strategies sharing infrastructure

HAIKU\_GB — the interesting one: Claude Haiku makes genuinely discretionary LONG/SHORT/FLAT calls on Gold and Brent, full reasoning, Python only enforces sizing/risk. No overlay telling it what to do.

What I actually found, not just what worked:

Only \~53% of my sandbox data turned out to be genuinely clean once I dug in — a mid-price logging bug had been quietly turning a real £220 loss into a fake £237 "profit" for eight weeks before I caught it

A rules overlay was silently vetoing \~half of Haiku's directional calls, which meant I was accidentally measuring "Haiku's judgment filtered through a rulebook" instead of Haiku's actual judgment

Found and fixed a fleet-crash bug that had been intermittently taking down the whole system for weeks — root cause was a Go binary (GitHub CLI) segfaulting under Android's sandboxed ptrace emulation

The most interesting pattern so far: my best entry-quality bot (61% win rate) is my worst performer overall, and my worst entry-quality bots (26-28% win rate) are flat-to-positive — exit management seems to matter more than entries, testing that hypothesis now with counterfactual logging

Current phase: spent the last month making the existing system honest before adding anything new — real broker reconciliation, fixed data integrity bugs, no new strategies. Targeting a clean data run through the end of the year, live money decision in January based on what the data actually shows, not vibes.

Happy to go deeper on any piece of this — the Haiku experiment, the bug-hunting, the architecture, whatever's interesting to people.

comments.author: TimothyWilliamProd
comments.body: Curious if you would share any of the v3 logic for trend/reversion detection. Big pain point for me right now.

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: I use ADX/Hurst regime filters on 4hr bars, running in Python. Execution's rigid, exits are rigid, ATR-based stops are rigid — no discretion in that part of the stack.

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: Hi. I asked all the other ai on my phone (I use them as a counsel) and they concluded it's reasoning speed and token burn were optimal for this type of work

replies.author: travelingthrwaway
replies.body: What is it reasoning exactly?  (Haiku isn’t great at reasoning for complex tasks.  Simple tasks might be better handled in a fully deterministic way, too.)

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: Haiku classifies the regime (trend/mean-revert/chop) off ADX/Hurst/ADF/Z-score, then produces a directional call with a confidence score. Once in a trade it re-evaluates every bar — I run it on both 30min and 4hr timeframes — asking itself whether the original thesis still holds. Exits are its own call, backstopped by a 3.0x ATR chandelier stop so a bad read doesn't run unchecked.

replies.author: travelingthrwaway
replies.body:
I see.  I have some similar approaches, but I’m only using Claude to build fully deterministic ML models that are then deployed.  No decisions are made by an LLM.    Claude helps me run my paper trading lab, iterate on models, evaluate results, etc.  It also keeps me honest by enforcing my own established criteria for declaring that something is an “improvement” vs. something that just looks like it might be good.  

It’s tough for the human brain to do that when the model may be evaluating dozens of features in milliseconds to establish an edge, but then represented in aggregate spread out over weeks of testing.  Claude helps me identify what market conditions have been tested in a live model deployment to paper trading vs. those that may exist in my long term history, that may be consequential for a model’s design, but absent in recent history.  It helps temper my excitement about lines that travel up and to the right on my charts ;)

Claude also helped me create a more realistic paper trading environment by correctly applying fees, considering the order book when placing a trade, slippage, etc.

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: Thanks for sharing. I'm a total coding novice. Over the last 8 months I've got a feeling for how to get the best out what I have. I am running this entirely from a Samsung tablet, a broker API and Claude/Claude code with 3 other ai as a counsel for some decision making.

replies.author: travelingthrwaway
replies.body: In my experience (outside of trading applications, even), Anthropic and OpenAI make resource allocation decisions that can change the behavior of the LLM.  This can happen even when you’ve made no changes to prompts, context, etc.  Haiku’s very limited IQ aside, I don’t think we can expect consistency from any hosted LLM if we don’t control all the levers.

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: True, I'm very cautious of each response I receive and often peer review complex stuff through the counsel. I've also set up a safety skill switch via a telegram API and also health reporting and status via natural language

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: I terested to know where you are at with your project and what you are wanting out of it?

replies.author: hikewithcaramel
replies.body: To answer the second part of your question. I have a fully deterministic bot running gold and Brent. The haiku bot is entirely experimental
